1:1.t: First, Chromatius, most learned of bishops, it is fitting for us to know that among the Greeks and Latins the name of the prophet is read corruptly as Ambacum, who among the Hebrews is called Habakkuk, and it is interpreted embrace, or, to render it more expressively in Greek, περίληψις, that is, embracing. Next, that where the Seventy translators and Symmachus and Theodotion translated λῆμμα, that is, assumption, in the Hebrew there stands massa, which Aquila translated as weight; on this we have argued more fully in the prophet Nahum. Massa, moreover, is never set at the head of a title except when what is seen is heavy and full of weight and toil. Hence the present prophecy too must have something of severity, so that, as in Nahum the weight that was seen against Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians, was heavy, so in this one also it may be asked for whom the weight is that is revealed to the prophet's sight. […]

1:2.t: What of Habakkuk? He utters more heated words, and is impatient with God Himself, and cries down, as it were our good Lord, because of the injustice of the judges. O Lord, how long shall I cry and Thou wilt not hear? Shall I cry out unto Thee of violence, and Thou wilt not save? Why dost Thou show me toil and labour, causing me to look upon perverseness and impiety? Judgment has been given against me, and the judge is a spoiler. Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth. Then comes the denunciation, and what follows upon it. Behold, ye despisers, and regard, and wonder marvellously, and vanish away, for I work a work. But why need I quote the whole of the denunciation?

How long, O Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I cry aloud to you, suffering violence, and will you not save? Why have you shown me iniquity and grief, to see plunder and injustice against me? LXX: How long, O Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I cry aloud to you, suffering violence, and will you not save? Why have you shown me toils and griefs, to see misery and impiety? Meanwhile, according to the letter, the prophet complains against God: why does Nebuchadnezzar lay waste the temple and Judah; why is Jerusalem, once the city of the Lord, destroyed? Why does the people cry out and is not heard? Why does it cry aloud to the Lord, oppressed by the Chaldeans, and is not saved? Why, too, has the prophet himself, or the people in whose person he now speaks, lived for this and been brought this far, to see the iniquity of the enemies and his own toil? Why does injustice prevail against him? […]

1:3.t:
And judgment has come about, and contradiction is the stronger.

Because of this the law is torn apart, and judgment does not come through to the end, because the wicked prevails against the just; therefore perverse judgment goes forth. LXX: Against me judgment has come about, and the judge takes; therefore the law is torn apart, and judgment does not come through to the end, because the wicked prevails against the just; therefore perverse judgment goes forth. The prophet or the people is still speaking to the Lord: that judgment was given against him not by truth but by power, and that he obtained nothing from the law and justice. Hence the judgment itself did not have its end. Now the end of judgment is to judge justly. And why he dares to say this he shows in what follows, saying: Because the wicked Nebuchadnezzar prevailed against the just Judah; […]

1:5.t: Look among the nations and see, and marvel, and be astounded, for a work has been done in your days which no one will believe when it is told. LXX: See, you despisers, and look, and marvel at marvels and perish, for I work a work in your days which you will not believe if anyone tells it. Symmachus, for what we have said, For a work has been done in your days, translated: For a work will be done in your days, the rest likewise. Again, at the beginning of the chapter, where in the Hebrew is written rau baggoim, and we translated Look among the nations, and the LXX put See, you despisers, while Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion agree with our translation, in a certain other edition, ἀνωνύμη (anonymous), I found: You will see the slanderers; and in another, likewise without the author's title: You will see those who turn aside. Therefore, to the earlier complaints of the prophet, who protests and says, How long, O Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? […]

This is Habakkuk the ninth in order, who was also privileged to speak concerning the resurrection of Christ in these terms: Behold, ye despisers, and regard, and wonder marvellously, and vanish for ever, because I work a work in your days which ye will not believe though it be told you. This passage Paul cited at Antioch of Pisidia as having reference to the resurrection of the Lord Christ.

1:6.t: Now let us come to the LXX, so that, setting out each sentence, we may fit to it the allegorical interpretation. Behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, which walks over the breadth of the earth, to possess tents not its own. God threatens the despisers and slanderers of his providence that he will raise up the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as it were demons; signifying either the most wicked angels, who minister to his fury and wrath and to the tribulation he brings upon sinners, or the souls of the most wicked men, through whom he torments those who deserve it. Now these Chaldeans are a bitter and swift nation, not sparing and quickly fulfilling what has been commanded them. And it walks over the breadth of the earth — for wide and spacious is the way that leads to death —, along which that rich man in the Gospel also walked, who shone in purple, and those of whom it is said: Who sleep on beds of ivory, and abound in luxuries on their couches. […]

For behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, walking over the breadth of the earth, to possess tents not its own. It is dreadful and terrible; from itself is judgment, and its burden will go forth. Its horses are lighter than leopards, and swifter than evening wolves; and its horsemen will spread abroad; for its horsemen will come from afar, they will fly like an eagle hastening to eat. All will come for plunder; their face is a burning wind; and it will gather captivity like sand. And he will triumph over kings, and tyrants will be his laughingstock; he will laugh at every fortress, and will heap up a mound, and will take it. Then the spirit will be changed, and he will pass through and fall; this is his strength, that of his god. LXX: For behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, which walks over the breadth of the earth, to possess tents not its own. It is terrible and illustrious; from itself will be its judgment, and its assumption will go forth from itself. […]

1:7.t: But as for what he says, From itself judgment and its burden will go forth, for which Symmachus translated, It will judge for itself, and will go forth by its own decree, it is to be understood either thus: it will appoint rulers from its own nation, and its power and its sword will have no attendants from other nations; or certainly: as it has done, so it will be done to it; and it will be laid waste just as it laid waste.

There follows: It is terrible and illustrious; from him will be its judgment, and its assumption will go forth from him. The Chaldean is terrible because of the many and varied punishments he brings upon the despisers; illustrious, because he takes to himself the glory of divinity. And through his oracles and false responses, and the cures of diseases which he himself had sent in, he seems illustrious among the ignorant and the despisers of God. For the judgment and punishment of the despiser will be from him, that is, from himself, or from the Chaldean. For according to the Apostle they will be handed over to him for punishment, that they may learn not to blaspheme; and whoever repents and is converted to God will go forth from him, though before he was held in his hands and was the assumption of the Chaldean. If ever we see that someone has served the devil for a long time, and afterwards has been converted to God, let us say of him: And his assumption has gone forth from him.

1:8.t: The horses also and the horsemen, who will come from afar, will be so quick to pursue and to lay everything waste that they will surpass leopards and evening wolves. For wolves are said to be fiercer as night draws near, roused to madness by hunger the whole day. The horsemen, then, will fly, not to fight, since no one will resist, but to range about like the eagle, to which everything among flying creatures is subject, hastening to devour.

For whoever repent and forsake the demons, to whom, like horses, they formerly offered their backs to be sat upon, and with the swiftness of leopards and of wolves at evening have thrown off and dashed down their riders, and have come with an empty and light back to carry him who, meek and poor, mounted the foal of an ass, these, as if hurrying from afar, and not content with running and rushing, will take to flight, and will come like an eagle, to feed on the flesh of the word of God and to satisfy the hunger of so long a time. For in what is said, Καὶ ἐξιππάζονται οἱ ἱππεῖς αὐτοῦ, which we too translated, And its horsemen will be ridden, according to the sense we set out above, Symmachus translated: Its horsemen will be poured out, that is, they will fall and be dashed to the ground. Now they are rightly called wolves of Arabia, that is, of evening and of the west, in whom a most wicked way of life has set, and who, once placed in darkness, abandon the evening with all their stride; […]

1:9.t: And just as at the blast of a burning wind all green things wither, so at the sight of them all things will be laid waste; and so great will be the number of captives and of plunder that, by ὑπερβολὴν (hyperbole), it could even be made equal to the sand.

And when these have been consumed, and the captivity snatched from their hands, then the divine word will gather like sand the captivity of the Chaldeans, and will take delight in kings, and tyrants will be its sport, seeing that the devil, once most powerful, and his kingdoms — showing which to the Savior also, he says, All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me —, have been destroyed by his coming; for it is the delight of prudence and the pleasure of wisdom when folly is destroyed, and the once great power of tyrants, overcome and cast down, is turned into derision. For not the dragon alone, who is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made a sport for the angels, was formed to be held in sport by the Lord; nor will God give him alone, like a sparrow to a little child; but if anyone else also is cruel and of a tyrannical mind, he will be handed over to the word of God for derision.

1:10.t: He too, that is, Nebuchadnezzar, will reign over the whole world, and, triumphing over kings before his chariot, he will hold them in derision and count them among his amusements; and he will be of such great power and pride that he will strive to overcome nature and to take the most strongly fortified cities by the might of his army. For he will come to Tyre, and, throwing a mound into the sea, he will make a peninsula of the island, and land will provide an entrance into the city between the waves of the sea. For this reason he will both laugh at every fortress, and heap up a mound, and take it, that is, the fortress, or Tyre; and this indeed is clearly shown in Ezekiel, where it is said: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, subjected his army to great labor against Tyre. Every head was bald, and every shoulder stripped of hair, and no wages were given to him and to his army against Tyre; and for the work in which he served against it.

And it says: He will make sport of every fortress. But what other fortress is there, except that of which the Apostle speaks: For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty for God for the destruction of fortresses, destroying thoughts, and every height that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God. If therefore there are any fortifications, either in discourses which promise that they have a height and greatness contrary to the truth, or in all the glory and riches and strength that is praised in the world, all will be destroyed, and the word of God will make sport of every fortress. And it will cast up a mound, and will take it by the mound and the earthly things it brings forward, convicting it of fragility in those things in which it formerly seemed to itself to have some strength.

1:11.t: And when he has heaped up a mound, and nothing has stood in the way of his strength, then his spirit will be changed into pride, and, believing himself to be God, he will set up a golden image in Babylon, which he will compel all the nations to worship. When he has done this, he will pass into the form of a beast, and afterwards will fall; for which Aquila and Symmachus translated καὶ πλημμελήσει, that is, and he will offend; holy Scripture having this custom, that it puts uasam, that is, he will offend, for what means: he will cease to be what he had been. We also have something of this kind in the idiom of our own language, when we say: The army has been beaten, for what means: it has been killed and cut down; and: The vineyard and the field have sinned, for what means: the vintage and the crops have had no yield. But what is said at the end of the chapter, This is his strength, that of his god, is to be read εἰρωνικῶς (ironically), so that the sense is: This is his strength, which Bel his god gave him. […]

And when this has been fulfilled, then the spirit will be turned, and will by no means punish as it had punished before, but, passing through the sinners, it will pray for them and reconcile them to their former Lord; in all of which is shown the strength of our God, which has accomplished such great things. You see how rugged the places are, and opposed to the truth of the history; and how the things we interpreted according to the letter concerning the Chaldeans now seem, according to tropology, to sound the clemency and liberty of those who have escaped from the hands of the Chaldeans. The history is strict and has no freedom to wander. Tropology is free, and bounded only by these laws: that it follow the piety of understanding and the context of the discourse, and not be violent in joining things that are greatly contrary to one another.

1:12.t: Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One? And shall we not die? O Lord, you have set him for judgment, and you have established him strong, that you might chastise. LXX: Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One? And shall we not die? O Lord, you have set him for judgment; and he has formed me, that I might reprove in his discipline. Symmachus more plainly: Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One, so that we should not die? O Lord, you have set him to judge, you have appointed him strong to chastise. To the complaint of the prophet, who said: How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? God had answered, saying: Look among the nations and see; and after this preface he had added: Behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation. And when the whole description was complete, whether of Nebuchadnezzar or of the devil, he recalls at the end: Then his spirit will be changed, and he will pass through, and he will fall; […]

1:13.t: But if we wish to understand it generally, of providence, the prophet asking: Why does the devil have so much power in the world, and, while God rules, another exercises tyranny? — the sense will be of this kind, and this exposition will be joined to what goes before: I know, O Lord my God, my Holy One, that because you provide and defend, we do not die, and I know that you have set the adversary for this reason, that through him, as through an executioner, you might chastise sinners and not slay them. I know that nothing unjust pleases you, and that your eyes are pure from all iniquity, and that you cannot look upon the sorrows of those who have been subjected to injustice. Yet I cannot find the cause why the unjust Cain kills the just Abel, and you are silent. Why, while the whale rages and devours everything, not only the smaller fish but also your own Jonah himself is devoured? Why does the wicked conquer, and the just is conquered? […]

Your eyes are pure, so that you may not see evil, and you will not be able to look upon iniquity. Why do you not look upon those who do iniquitous things, and are silent while the wicked devours one more just than himself. And you will make men like the fish of the sea, and like a creeping thing that has no prince? LXX: The eye is pure, so that it may not see evils, and you will not be able to look upon sorrow. Why do you look upon the despisers, will you be silent when the wicked has devoured one more just than himself? And you will make men like the fish of the sea, and like creeping things that have no leader. Jeremiah too says something of this kind to God: You are just, O Lord, I confess; yet I will speak judgments to you: Why is it that the way of the wicked prospers; that all abound who transgress and do wrong? You planted them and they have taken root, they have begotten sons and have borne fruit; you are near to their mouth, and far from their reins. […]

1:14.t: Otherwise, how can God so hold men as the fish of the sea, and as creeping things that have no prince, when the angels of each one daily see the face of the Father who is in heaven, and the angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him, and delivers them? Just as, therefore, among men the providence of God runs even through each individual, so in the other animals we can understand a general dispensation, indeed, and order, and course of things. For example, how the multitude of fish is born and lives in the waters, how creeping things and four-footed beasts arise on the earth, and by what foods they are nourished. But it is absurd to bring down the majesty of God to this, that he should know at each moment how many gnats are born, or how many die, what multitude of bugs and fleas and flies there is on the earth, how many fish swim about in the water, and which of the smaller ought to yield as prey to the larger. […]

1:15.t: He lifted up the whole with a hook, he dragged it in his dragnet, and gathered it into his net; over this he will rejoice and exult. Therefore he will sacrifice to his dragnet, and offer sacrifice to his net; because through them his portion has been made fat, and his food choice. For this reason, therefore, he spreads out his dragnet, and never ceases always to slay the nations. LXX: He lifted up the consummation with a hook, and drew it in his net, and gathered it in his dragnets. For this reason he will rejoice and be glad; therefore he will sacrifice to his dragnet, and burn incense to his net, because through them he has made his portion fat, and his foods are choice. Therefore he spreads out his net, and never ceases always to slay the nations. […]

1:16.t: And SO it is most clearly established by instances and testimonies from Scripture that the mischief of pride, although it comes later in the order of the combat, is yet earlier in origin, and is the beginning of all sins and faults: nor is it (like the other vices) simply fatal to the virtue opposite to it (in this case, humility), but it is also at the same time destructive of all virtues: nor does it only tempt ordinary folk and small people, but chiefly those who already stand on the heights of valour. For thus the prophet speaks of this spirit, "His meat is choice."
1:16.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 12, Chapter 6

2:1.t: I will stand upon my watch, and fix my step upon the fortification, and I will look out, to see what is said to me and what I may answer to the one who reproves me. LXX: I will stand upon my watch, and I will go up upon the rock, and I will look out, to see what he speaks in me, and what I may answer to my correction. Symmachus has followed it out more plainly: Like a watchman I will stand upon the lookout, and I will stand as one shut in, and I will look out, to see what is said to me, and what I may answer, and gainsay against the one who reproves me. For fortification and rock, in place of which Symmachus translated shut in, there is put in the Hebrew masur, which Theodotion translated circuit, Aquila and the Fifth Edition compass. To the first complaint the Lord had answered: Look among the nations and see, and wonder and be astonished. To which the prophet, as though doing penance for what he had said before, had indeed moderated his question, saying: O Lord my God, my Holy One, and we shall not die. […]

Where, then, did I find you in order to learn about you? For you were not already in my memory before I learned of you. Where, then, did I find you in order to learn about you, unless in yourself above me? Yet there is no place. We go backward and we go forward, yet there is no place. O truth, you do preside over all things, even those that take counsel with you, and you do answer in the same time all who consult you, however diverse their questions. You do answer clearly, but all do not hear clearly. All seek counsel concerning what they wish, but they do not always hear what they wish. He serves you best who does not so much expect to hear the thing from you that he himself desires, but rather to desire what he hears from you.

And therefore by him who is exercising anxious care over the purity of his inner man, those districts should be sought, which do not by their fruitfulness and fertility invite his mind to the trouble of cultivating them, nor drive him forth from his fixed and immovable position in his cell, and force him to go forth to some work in the open air, and so, his thoughts being as it were poured forth openly, scatter to the winds all his concentration of mind and all the keenness of his vision of his aim. And this cannot be guarded against or seen by anyone at all however careful and watchful, except one who continually keeps his body and soul shut up and enclosed in walls, that, like a splendid fisherman, looking out for food for himself by the apostolic art, he may eagerly and without moving catch the swarms of thoughts swimming in the calm depths of his heart, and surveying with curious eye the depths as from a high rock, may sagaciously and cunningly decide what he ought to lure to himself by his saving hook, and what […]

2:2.t: The all-merciful and beneficent Father has [a heart for] those who fear him, and kindly and lovingly he bestows his favors upon those who come to him with a simple mind. Therefore let us not be double-minded; neither let our soul be lifted up on account of his exceedingly great and glorious gifts. Far from us be that which is written, "Wretched are they who are of a double mind and of a doubting heart; who say, 'These things we have heard even in the times of our fathers, but, behold, we have grown old, and none of them has happened unto us.' " You foolish ones! Compare yourselves with a tree; take the vine. First of all, it sheds its leaves, then it buds, next it puts forth leaves, and then it flowers; afterwards comes the sour grape, and then follows the ripened fruit. You perceive how in a little time the fruit of a tree comes to maturity. […]

According to the promise which is made to the holy man in Isaiah, saying: While you are still speaking, I will say, Behold, I am here, now too the Lord answered the prophet, and commanded him to write the vision and to set her out upon tablets, that is, to write more plainly. But I think the tablets are those of which the Apostle also speaks to the Corinthians: You are our letter, written in our hearts, which is known and read by all men; being made manifest that you are the letter of Christ, ministered by us, and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on fleshly tablets of the heart. And Solomon too signifies something of the kind in Proverbs, saying: Write her upon the breadth of your heart. And he is commanded to write more plainly, so that the reader may be able to run, and his speed and his desire of reading may be held back by no hindrance.

But what he says is of this kind, provided only that we mix in the translation of the Seventy too. Write in your heart; and as little children who receive the first elements of letters train their crooked strokes and trembling hand on boxwood, and by practice grow used to writing correctly, so you too, who have spoken in the person of the doubting people, write what I say on the tablets of your heart and on the boxwood of your breast. For it is a vision which is promised and which is commanded to be set out and written more plainly, so that it may be wrapped in no cloud and obscured by no windings of riddles; let a clear hope have a clear pledge. […]

However, I am not unaware that according to their translation it can also be taken thus: Write the vision in which Christ is promised, and, whether on boxwood, or on tablets, or, as Symmachus translated, on pages, weave this discourse of your prophecy: that at the appointed time and at the consummation of the world my Son will come, to save the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and to join other sheep also to the ancient sheep, and, making one flock, to join the two rods, which Ezekiel, that is, the strength of God, holds joined and cleaving to one another in his prophetic hand. But if, O prophet, or you, O people — in whose person my prophet also seemed to doubt —, Christ withdraws himself a little and seems to delay, wait for him; for coming he will come, and will not tarry, and the rest which we have already expounded above.

And the Lord answered me, and said: Write the vision, and make him plain upon tablets, that he who reads him may run through; for the vision is still far off, and he will appear at the end, and will not lie; if he delays, wait for him, for coming he will come, and will not tarry. Behold, he who is unbelieving, his soul will not be upright in himself. But the just shall live in his faith. LXX: And the Lord answered to me, and said: Write the vision, and plainly on boxwood, that he who reads may pursue these things; for the vision is still for a time, and will rise at the end, and not in vain. If he fails, wait for him, for coming he will come and will not tarry; if he draws himself back, it will not please my soul in him. But the just shall live by my faith. For tablets and boxwood, which in Hebrew is called alluoth, Symmachus translated pages. And where the Seventy put: But the just shall live by my faith, all alike translated, shall live by his faith. […]

Moreover, as to what we translated for vision: For the vision is still far off, and if he delays, wait for him, that is, the vision (uisum), let no one, deceived by error, think that I put uisus, which is masculine and less usual in Latin, for uisio, which is feminine. For hazon, which Aquila translates ὁραματισμὸν (vision), is called among the Hebrews uisus, in the masculine gender, and to the end, under the same gender of the vision, that is, of uisus, the masculine inflection is kept. But the Seventy, saying: Write the vision, and afterwards: If he fails, wait for him; for coming he will come, and will not tarry; if he withdraws himself, it will not please my soul in him, first translated uisio in the feminine gender, which among the Hebrews, as we have said, is masculine. Then, following the Hebrew gender, where it is inflected in the masculine, wait for him, and it will not please my soul in him, they too inflected it in the masculine gender. […]

Of what else than the advent of Christ, who was to come, is Habakkuk understood to say, "And the Lord answered me, and said, 'Write the vision openly on a tablet of boxwood so that the one who reads these things may understand.' " For the vision is yet for a time appointed, and it will arise in the end, and it will not become void. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and will not be delayed.

2:3.t:
[Passage quoted, Hab. ii. 2.]

AND here it is clearly foretold that the subject of the prophecy who is coming will come. Who could this be but he who is referred to above in the words, "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord, the Lord God also has shone upon us"? With which also Zechariah agrees, when he says: "Behold a man, the Dawn is his name, and he shall rise from below." The same prophet, too, noting the time adds, "At eventide it shall be light. If he delays, wait for him." Instead of which Aquila reads, "If he tarry expect him, for he that cometh will come, and will not tarry." And the Epistle to the Hebrews has this in mind when it says:

"Cast not away then your confidence, which has great recompense of reward. For ye have need of patience, that, doing the will of God, ye may receive the promise. For yet a little while, and he that cometh will come, and will not tarry. And the just shall live by my faith. And if he draw back, my soul hath no pleasure in him." […]
2:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 14

2:3.t: And he commands this because the vision is still far off, and set in an appointed time. And when the end of things has come, then he too will come, and the prophecy will be proved true, fulfilled in deed. But if perhaps, through your desire, O reader, and your ardor to see the vision, what has been promised should seem to you to delay a little, do not despair of its coming, but wait patiently: for you have me, who promise you and say: Coming he will come, and will not tarry.

But the vision itself, of which I said to you: Write the vision, and make it plain on boxwood, that he who reads may be able to pursue, is still set in an appointed time, of which the Savior says: In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. And it will rise at the consummation of the world, and in the last hour of the day, of which John also speaks: Little children, now it is the last hour, and it will not come in vain; for it will save many, and with the remnant of the Israelite people it will gather a multitude of the nations. But if she withdraws herself a little, and the vision begins to come more slowly than your wishes, O reader, who are commanded to read on the boxwood and on the tablets which the prophet wrote out, wait for her, for coming she will come, and will not tarry.

2:4.t: "And if you will not believe, neither will you understand." Also the Lord in the Gospel: "For if you believe not that I am he, you shall die in your sins." Moreover, righteousness should subsist by faith. In it was life, as predicted in Habakkuk: "Now the just shall live by faith in me." Hence Abraham, the father of the nations, believed. In Genesis "Abraham believed in God, and it was counted to him for righteousness." In like manner Paul wrote to the Galatians: "Abraham 'believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.' So you see, those of faith are the descendants of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.' So then, those who are people of faith are blessed with Abraham who had faith."
2:4.s: Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 12:1.5

2:4.t: How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. […]
2:4.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: HOW THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM WAS FULFILLED IN CHRIST

2:4.t:
But since in the Law no one is justified before God, it is manifest that the righteous lives by faith. But the Law is not of faith, but he who has done these things shall live in them.

The example by which it is proved that the righteous lives by faith, and not by works, he took from Habakkuk, which the Seventy translators rendered thus: "But the righteous lives by my faith" (Hab. 2:4). Aquila and Theodotion: "But the righteous lives by his faith", that is, God's. It must therefore be considered that he did not say "a human being" or "a man lives by faith", lest he should give occasion for despising the works of the virtues; but the righteous lives by faith: so that whoever was faithful and was to live through faith could not otherwise come to faith, or live in it, unless he had first been righteous, and had ascended by purity of life as by certain steps to faith. It can therefore happen that someone is righteous, and yet does not live, being without faith in Christ. […]

But if anyone is unbelieving of this pledge of mine, and while I say: Coming he will come, and will not tarry, begins to doubt and to waver silently within himself, thinking that what delays for a time will not come, this man will displease my soul, according to that saying: Your new moons and sabbaths my soul hates. But that God spoke of his soul, we ought to take for mind and thought, so that the meaning is: he will displease my sense. And just as he will displease who, when I promise, doubts that what I pledge will come, so the just man who believes my promise will live in his faith. With these lines, as it were, the picture of this chapter has been sketched.

But if your faith doubts, and you think that what I pledge will not come to pass, you will have it as a great punishment that you will displease my soul. But the just man, who believes my words and does not doubt the things I promise, will have as reward life everlasting. Nor ought you at once to charge, either in my slaying you or in my giving life to him, that there is respect of persons with me; for he himself is the cause of his own giving of life, who lives by his faith, just as you, by having withdrawn yourself and refused to believe, have displeased my soul. And in these words there is plainly a prophecy of the coming of Christ. Hence the question that was put forward is also solved: that until he comes, iniquity rules in the world, and judgment does not come to its end, and the true Nebuchadnezzar catches men with his net and dragnet like little fish, and the rational animal like a creeping thing that has no prince.

Moreover, why the Apostle, writing to the Romans, made use rather of the testimony of the LXX, But the just shall live by my faith, and not of what is found in the Hebrew, the reason is plain. For he was writing to Romans, who did not know the Hebrew Scriptures; nor was he concerned about the words, since the sense was safe, and the present argument suffered no harm from it. Otherwise, wherever the sense is different, and it is written one way in the Hebrew and another in the LXX, note that he uses those testimonies which he had learned from Gamaliel, the teacher of the law.

Let no one therefore, dearly beloved, flatter himself on any merits of a good life, if works of charity be wanting in him, and let him not trust in the purity of his body, if he be not cleansed by the purification of almsgiving. For “almsgiving wipes out sin,” kills death, and extinguishes the punishment of perpetual fire. But he who has not been fruitful therein, shall have no indulgence from the great Recompenser, as Solomon says, “He that closeth his ears lest he should hear the weak, shall himself call upon the Lord, and there shall be none to hear him.” And hence Tobias also, while instructing his son in the precepts of godliness, says, “Give alms of thy substance, and turn not thy face from any poor man: so shall it come to pass that the face of God shall not be turned from thee.” This virtue makes all virtues profitable; […]

A mighty bulwark is a sound faith, a true faith, to which nothing has to be added or taken away: because unless it is one, it is no faith, as the Apostle says, “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all.” Cling to this unity, dearly beloved, with minds unshaken, and in it “follow after” all “holiness,” in it carry out the Lord’s commands, because “without faith it is impossible to please God,” and without it nothing is holy, nothing is pure, nothing alive: “for the just lives by faith,” and he who by the devil’s deception loses it, is dead though living, because as righteousness is gained by faith, so too by a true faith is eternal life gained, as says our Lord and Saviour. And this is life eternal, that they may know Thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom Thou hast sent.

It should be noted that the Church was placed in paradise, like the first man, "to till it," in such a way that no one would say "that anything he possessed" was "his own." For it began in a state of great perfection that is observed today in the religious life, for the love of Christ was still recent, and in those days "a large number also of the priests accepted the faith." This Church, meaning the one that began with the Jews, because they were converted at one time by the three thousand, and at another, by the five thousand, possessed the "tree of life," that is, faith, because "My just one lives by faith." It also had the "tree of knowledge," that is, the Law, which remained with them for seeing and reading, and not for eating. Much more: for "the day you eat of it, you must die." And so you may see the tree of knowledge, but not eat of it, or else you would destroy what Christ had done; and death would necessarily come in, for "the letter kills." […]

2:5.t: Since, therefore, the Lord thus threatens such shepherds through whom the sheep of the Lord are neglected and perish, what else ought we to do, dearly beloved brother, but to show full diligence in collecting and restoring the sheep of Christ and to apply the medicine of paternal piety to care for the wounds of the lapsed? The Lord also in the Gospel warns and says, "It is not the healthy who need a physician, but they who are sick." For although we shepherds are many, yet we feed one flock. All of the sheep whom Christ sought by his blood and passion we ought to embrace and to cherish, and not to allow our suppliant and grieving brothers to be cruelly despised and to be trodden under foot by the proud presumption of certain ones, since it is written, "The man, however, who is stiff-necked, boastful of himself, will accomplish nothing at all. His greed is as wide as Sheol."

And as wine deceives the one who drinks it, so will the proud man be, and he will not be adorned; who has enlarged his soul like hell, and he himself is like death, and is not filled. And he will gather to himself all nations, and will heap up to himself all peoples. Will not all these take up a parable against him, and the speech of his riddles, and it will be said: Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own, how long does he also weigh down thick clay against himself? Will not those suddenly rise up who bite you, and those who tear you be stirred up, and you will be for a plunder to them? Because you have despoiled many nations, all who are left of the peoples will despoil you, because of the blood of man, and the iniquity of the land, of the city and of all who dwell in it. LXX: But he who is arrogant and a despiser, a proud man, brings nothing to completion; who has enlarged his soul like hell, and he is like death, he is not filled. […]

Let us examine the Seventy as well. All that we have said of Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar can be referred to this world and to the devil, who, truly arrogant and proud, and believing himself to be something, will bring nothing to completion. For indeed his endeavor and all his labor will come to destruction, he who, in the likeness of hell and of death, is not sated with the slain, and rejoices in the deception of all nations, and gathers peoples to himself.

This same thing can also be interpreted of the Antichrist, who will be so arrogant and proud that he will sit in the temple of God, making himself God. And like hell and death he will slay so many, and gather so many to himself, that, if it were possible, he would deceive even the elect of God. He will also gather to himself all nations, so as to lead all peoples into his error.

We can also, according to the apostle John — who writes: As you have heard that the Antichrist is coming, but now there are many antichrists; whence we also know that it is the last hour —, call arrogant and proud all heretics and every perverse doctrine of those who claim knowledge for themselves and despise the simplicity of the Church, who bring nothing to completion but take delight in the deaths of very many; and adapt the whole content of the chapter to an understanding concerning them, who truly multiply for themselves what is not their own, and, gathering to themselves as it were very heavy clay and a weighty collar by which they may be dragged to punishment, despoil many nations, and shed the blood of men, and exercise impiety against the Church and against all its inhabitants. But the remaining peoples, namely churchmen, who have not been deceived by their error, will suddenly rise up and awake as from a heavy sleep, and will bite them, and will lay snares for them, and will have them as a prey.

2:6.t: When he has been made drunk with the cup of the Lord and lulled to sleep by the undiluted chalice, will not all speak over him by way of comparison, a πρόβλημα (a riddle)? Woe to him who, laying waste the whole world, is not sated with plunder, and does not cease to despoil those already stripped, and rages only to this end, that he may devour, and presses himself down with the burden of iniquity and of spoils as with a very heavy collar. And at the same time consider how elegantly he has called multiplied riches thick clay.

When they see him sent into the abyss and handed over to Tartarus, seeing fulfilled the things which they had read in the prophets in parables and αἰνιγματωδῶς (in riddles), and interpreting them concerning him, they will recount with one harmonious voice: Woe to the devil, who has multiplied for himself what is not his own. Woe to the partridge, which has gathered what it did not bring forth. How long? This is either the voice of those who rebuke, or of those who point to the day of judgment. And weighing down his collar with infinite weight. And beautifully: since he is arrogant and proud — and pride is properly shown in the stretching out of the neck and the raising of the nape —, the collar is very heavy, so as to bend what had been raised up.

Some think that what is said: Woe to those who multiply for themselves the things that are not their own, and the rest, can be taken of rich men, who extend the boundaries of their possessions and, thinking that the things which are not man's are man's, gather to themselves things by which they will suddenly be left. But that earthly possession is not man's, that is, not the rational animal's, the Lord too shows, saying: If you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is your own? And they expound the whole tenor of the chapter of this person. But I do not know whether they can keep the order of the prophetic question and solution.

When afterwards they see him slain by the breath of Christ's mouth, they will understand that the things foretold of him beforehand are true, and they will say all that follows, with the same understanding with which we have expounded it concerning the devil. As for what he says, all the remaining peoples will despoil you because of the blood of men and the impiety of the land, and of the city and of all who dwell in it, let us understand the remaining peoples as the holy ones who did not serve the Antichrist; by whom the impious one will be despoiled because of the impiety which he exercised against the whole earth, and the laying waste of the city of the Church, and the persecution of all who have dwelt in it. […]

God also makes mention of them by the voice of Jeremiah, saying of the enemy of all, even Satan; "Woe to him, who multiplieth for himself that which is not his, and maketh his collar thick and heavy: for suddenly shall they arise that shall bite him, and thy adversaries shall wake up, and thou shalt be their prey." For Satan had gathered unto him all the inhabitants of the earth, though they were not his, and had caused them to be his worshippers, making his collar heavy: but those who were to plunder his goods woke up: for the net of the apostolic teaching caught all those that were in error, and brought back unto God the whole world.
2:6.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

2:7.t: And this will come about because suddenly those will rise up who bite him: either the angels with whom the devil will be handed over to punishment, or those who had been tempted by him and afterwards do penance; and, turned to the standards of Christ, they will bite him, according to what is said elsewhere: Your men of peace have laid snares for you. Then follows: And your ambushers will awake, that is, you will lie exposed to the snares of those whom you had earlier lulled to sleep, whom you had made drunk, as they lay waste your kingdom and bring back those who were captives into the troops of Christ.

Will not the Medes and Persians suddenly rise up, who, destroying the empire of the Babylonians, will bite him first and afterwards tear him; and will not Nebuchadnezzar become a plunder for them, and the ravager of the whole world be despoiled by the remaining peoples, who were able to escape his hand and his cruelty? But this will happen to him because of the blood of man, that is, of Judah, and the iniquity of the land, namely of Israel, and of the city, doubtless Jerusalem, and of all who dwell in it, signifying the people in general.

And yet in old time he had said: "I will hold the whole world in my hand as a nest, and will take it as eggs that are left: and there is no one that shall escape from me, or speak against me." He missed, then, the truth, and fell from his hope, proud and audacious though he was, and vaunting himself over the infirmity of mankind. For the Lord of powers marshalled against him the ministers of the sacred proclamations. And this verily had been foretold by one of the holy prophets when speaking of Satan and the holy teachers: "That suddenly they shall arise that bite thee: and they shall awake that afflict thee, and thou shalt be their prey." For, so to speak, they bit Satan by attacking his glory, and making his goods a spoil, and bringing them unto Christ by means of faith in Him: for so they attacked Satan himself.
2:7.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

2:8.t: For you have plundered many nations, and have stripped the Jewish people of the adornment and the garments which I had given it; therefore all the remaining peoples, who have not bowed their neck to your rule, will despoil you and make you naked. For you too have slain very many nations and have shed their blood. But also the impiety of the land, that is, of the land of the Jews, and of the city of Jerusalem, and of all its inhabitants, who said against their Creator: Crucify, crucify him; his blood be upon us and upon our children, will return upon your head and will be the causes of your despoiling.

2:9.t: Woe to him who gathers an evil avarice for his house, so that his nest may be on high, and who thinks he is freed from the hand of evil. You have devised confusion for your house, you have cut down many peoples, and your soul has sinned. For the stone will cry out from the wall, and the timber that is between the joints of the buildings will answer. LXX: O he who multiplies an evil avarice for his house, so as to set his nest on high, and to be rescued from the hand of evils. You have devised confusion for your house, you have consumed many peoples; and your soul has sinned, for which reason the stone will cry out from the wall, and the beetle from the wood will speak these things. The discourse is still addressed to him who heaps up evils for himself and does not understand that the multitude of his riches is the cause of the ruin of his house; […]

What their translation means we shall say in the exposition of the Seventy translators, in whom O is put for woe, and the discourse is directed either to the devil or to the Antichrist, or to the heretics, who multiply an evil avarice for themselves. Now avarice is called evil to distinguish it from good avarice, so that there is a good avarice of the churchly teacher, who is never sated with the multitude of his followers, and the more disciples he has, the more he is roused to zeal for teaching. Woe, therefore, to him who multiplies for himself a most wicked avarice, so as to gather perverse conventicles for his house, and to set his nest on high, so as to be rescued from the hand of evils. For the devil and the Antichrist and the heretics promise that those who accept their doctrine will be in the heavenly places and will possess the kingdoms of heaven, and will not feel the fires of Gehenna.

2:10.t: And though they have promised these things, their counsel will not be able to come to completion; but it will be a counsel of confusion and ignominy for their house, after the very end of things has shown to be false what had been promised, when it is proved to be a counsel of confusion, not of salvation. This teacher of perversity, as we have said, has consumed many peoples, and the more he had in his company, the more he sinned against his own soul.

You have slain many peoples, and in killing others you have raged against your own soul, and you have run riot in such cruelty that, if it can be said, the stones of the city and the timbers of the walls which you have overthrown cry out your ferocity. Something of this kind the Lord too said in the Gospel against the Pharisees, who reproached him for not rebuking the children who acclaimed him: Hosanna in the highest to the son of David, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest. Have you not read, he says, that it is written: Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise? And if these are silent, the stones will cry out. […]

2:11.t: Then the stones of his church, and the κάνθαρος, that is, the beetle from the wood, will cry out against the avarice of the proud one, because he has deceived all nations by his persuasion. By the stones we can understand the dull hearts of those who believe the doctrines of the heretics, and by the beetle from the wood, all perverse masters who, taking up the preaching of the cross for the sake of shameful gain, speak from the belly. For their god is their belly, and they do all things for the sake of food, which is turned into dung — for the beetle or cantharus is a dung worm —, and they take up the cross only for this, that with viperous mouth they may teach the avarice and pride of their master the devil. If ever you see one of the heretics speaking against the Church as if of hidden and secret mysteries, and preferring the house of the devil to the house of Christ, say: The stone cries out from the wall, and the cantharus speaks from the wood. […]

2:12.t: Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed, and prepares a town in iniquity. Are not these things from the Lord of hosts? For peoples will labor in much fire, and nations in vain, and they will fail; for the earth will be filled, so that they may know the glory of the Lord, like waters covering the sea. LXX: Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed, and prepares a town in iniquities. Are not these things from the Lord Almighty? And many peoples have failed in fire, and many nations have been straitened, for the earth will be filled so that it may know the glory of the Lord, like water to cover the seas. No one doubts that according to the letter the prophetic discourse is still speaking against Nebuchadnezzar, and lamenting him because he builds Babylon with bloodshed, and constructs its walls with the ruin and death of very many.

But it is clear that the devil, and the Antichrist, and the perverse doctrine of the heretics build a city with bloodshed, that is, their own church on the destruction of those whom they have deceived, and prepare a town in iniquities, speaking iniquity against God and setting their mouth on high. And when they have done this, it is plainly shown that they build the city of themselves with bloodshed, and prepare it in iniquities.

It can also be understood — although it does not suit the order of the reading, nor fit the present text of Scripture — of Jerusalem, the city full of the blood of the prophets, of which Scripture records that the blood of the saints overflowed in it from gate to gate. And which says at the Lord's passion: His blood be upon us and upon our children. And to which God speaks in Isaiah: When you lift up your hands to me, I will not hear you; for your hands are full of blood. This city was built in iniquities, in which, according to the same prophet, justice slept.

2:13.t: And because he did this to the city which he had built with bloodshed, he afterwards hears what is brought upon him by the Lord. For there follows: Are not these things from the Lord of hosts? That is, the things that are said: Peoples will labor in much fire, and nations in vain; that is, when Babylon has been burned, the peoples will labor in vain and strive for nothing, and the peoples of the Chaldean nation will fail.

For there follows: Are not these things from the Lord Almighty? That is, such a building is not from the Lord Sabaoth, whom the LXX have here translated Almighty. For many peoples will fail, and although countless nations are led into their error, yet either they will grow weary, which ὠλιγοψύχησαν (they lost heart) rather signifies, or at any rate they will be pressed into a narrow space, and will not be able to be compared with the multitude of the Church. For while they fail in the fire, — which is understood either as their being consumed by the fire of the devil, their prince, or as their being kindled by the fire of the Lord, of which he says: I came to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it may burn, and drawn back from their former course, and doing penance, and abandoning the journey they had begun, which is what ὀλιγοψυχία (faintheartedness) means —; […]

Nor is its building from the Lord Sabaoth. Hence also many peoples failed in fire, and many nations grew weary at the time when it was surrounded by the armies of Vespasian and Titus, and those who came for the solemn day of the Passover were shut up in the city as in a prison, and failed through famine and want, and the siege of Hadrian brought them to the final ruins. And when the city of bloodshed and the town of iniquities had been overthrown, and the peoples consumed by fire, and the nations which had come to their help scattered this way and that and letting fall their weary hands, the whole earth was filled with the glory of Christ, and as with waters, so with his words and teaching the whole world was covered.

2:14.t: For the earth will be filled so that it may know the glory of the Lord, that is, when Babylon has been overthrown, the might of God's power will become manifest to all; like waters covering the sea, so the whole earth will be filled with the glory of the Lord, just as the waters cover the bed and the bottom of the sea. These things, as we have said, are according to the letter.

2:15.t: What, then, must we do, who have received from Paul, the teacher of the Church, institutions of understanding of this kind? Does it not seem just that we should keep the rule of this kind handed down to us by a like example in the rest? Or shall we, as certain people wish, forsaking these things which so great and such an Apostle handed down, turn back again to "Jewish fables"? For my part, if I should expound these things otherwise than as they seem to Paul, I think this is to give a hand to the enemies of Christ, and this is what the prophet says: "Woe to him who gives his neighbor to drink with turbulent overthrow!" Having therefore received from the blessed Apostle Paul the seeds of spiritual understanding, let us cultivate them, insofar as the Lord shall deign to enlighten us through your prayers.

What of Habakkuk? He utters more heated words, and is impatient with God Himself, and cries down, as it were our good Lord, because of the injustice of the judges. O Lord, how long shall I cry and Thou wilt not hear? Shall I cry out unto Thee of violence, and Thou wilt not save? Why dost Thou show me toil and labour, causing me to look upon perverseness and impiety? Judgment has been given against me, and the judge is a spoiler. Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth. Then comes the denunciation, and what follows upon it. Behold, ye despisers, and regard, and wonder marvellously, and vanish away, for I work a work. But why need I quote the whole of the denunciation? A little further on, however, for I think it best to add this to what has been said, after upbraiding and lamenting many of those who are in some respect unjust or depraved, he upbraids the leaders and teachers of wickedness, stigmatising vice as a foul disorder, and an intoxication and aberration of mind; […]

Woe to him who gives drink to his friend, putting in his gall and making him drunk, that he may look upon his nakedness. He is filled with shame instead of glory; drink, you also, and fall into a stupor. The cup of the right hand of the Lord will surround you, and the vomit of shame will be upon your glory, for the iniquity of Lebanon will cover you, and the devastation of the cattle will terrify them, because of the blood of men and the iniquity of the land, and of the city and of all who dwell in it. LXX: Woe to him who offers drink to his neighbor with a turbid overturning, and makes him drunk, that he may look into their caves; a fill of shame from glory drink, you also, and be shaken. The cup of the right hand of the Lord has surrounded you, and shame has been gathered upon your glory, for the impiety of Lebanon will cover you, and the misery of the beasts will terrify you, because of the blood of men, and the impieties of the land and of the city, and of all who dwell in it. […]

But let us come to the spiritual understanding. Woe to you, devil, or Antichrist, or perverse doctrine of the heretics, who with your teachings and your turbid potion make drunk the peoples of the deceived, and overturn their former faith, giving them a potion not from Siloam, not from the Jordan, not from the springs of Israel, but from the brook Kidron, and from the river of Egypt, of which Jeremiah says: What have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you should drink the water of Gihon? For this in the Hebrew is written sior, that is, turbid and muddy; for although the rivers of Egypt are believed to go out from the paradise of the Scriptures, yet because they are trampled by the feet of Pharaoh, they have lost their splendor, and, defiled by the Egyptian mud, have been turned into torrents, at having escaped which the holy one rejoices, saying: Our soul has passed through the torrent. […]

Now these things are said through the metaphor of a drunken man, disgraced by nakedness, because Nebuchadnezzar made all men drunk with the cup of his fury, and saw them all stripped and captive, and those who had once been glorious were reduced to the utmost slavery; for this is what he says: He is filled with shame instead of glory, so that we supply "the friend" and "the neighbor", or the partner in the kingdom, who drank your cup, O Nebuchadnezzar. Hence, because you have made very many drunk, you also drink from the cup of the Lord and fall into a stupor; you will be surrounded by the punishments of the right hand of the Lord, and with the shame of your vomit you will discharge all that you had swallowed, and from lofty glory you will be brought down to the utmost evils.

I heard at Lydda one of the Hebrews, who was called a wise man among them and a δευτερώτης (a teacher of the traditions), telling a tale of this sort: Zedekiah, he said, blinded by King Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, that is, Antioch, and mocked in various ways, was led to Babylon. There, when one day Nebuchadnezzar was celebrating the festivities of a banquet, he ordered a potion to be given to him which, once drained, would loosen the drinker's belly into a flux; and Zedekiah, suddenly brought in before the faces of the banqueters and compelled by the force of his belly, was befouled with excrement; and this, he said, is what Scripture now says here: Woe to him who gives drink to his friend, putting in his gall and making him drunk, that he may look upon his nakedness, and shame instead of glory; namely, that he who had been a most powerful king was brought by him to such disgrace. Hence God also threatens him that he himself will drink a potion of this sort, and suffer everything that Zedekiah suffered. […]

But if we wish to understand it of the Antichrist, or of the devil who will work in the Antichrist, he too, with his cup, with which he will desire to overturn the discipline of Christ, will make very many drunk, so that, drunk, they enter his caves; but after the end has come, instead of that glory with which he had magnified himself, he will be filled with shame. And he will be filled, because he will drink the cup of punishments, and he will be shaken, in no way firm in his malice, but trembling, and repenting too late. For the cup of the right hand of the Lord will surround him, the Lord who is also the Savior, when he slays him with the spirit of his mouth and destroys him with the illumination of his coming. Then all the shame which he gathered for himself by thoughts, deeds and words will come upon his glory, so that as renowned as he was formerly thought, so full of shame he will afterward be. […]

So then it is of no good to hold one's tongue, if we impose silence upon ourselves for this reason that by our silence we may do what would have been done by an outcry on our part, simulating certain gestures by which he whom we ought to have cured, may be made still more angry, while we are commended for all this, to his loss and damage: as if a man were not for this very reason the more guilty, because he tried to get glory for himself out of his brother's fall. For such a silence will be equally bad for both because while it increases the vexation in the heart of another, so it prevents it from being removed from one's own: and against such persons the prophet's curse is with good reason directed: "Woe to him that giveth drink to his friend, and presenteth his gall, and maketh him drunk, that he may behold his nakedness. He is filled with shame instead of glory."
2:15.s: The First Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 18

2:16.t: After this follows: A fill of shame instead of glory drink, you, and be shaken, that is: O devil, O perverse doctrine, O heretic, who thought yourself a golden cup with which all the nations are made drunk, so that they might see your caves and your secrets, instead of the greatness of your glory be filled with a fill of shame, and be reckoned as an earthen vessel, the works of the potter's hands; drink, you also, from the cup of the Lord, of which it is said in the psalm: A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed, and he has tilted it from this into that; yet its dregs have not been emptied out. And be shaken from your former opinion, and do not think firm and stable the things in which you at first desired to stand, because the cup of the right hand of the Lord has surrounded you.

Moreover, because you offered drink to your neighbor with a turbid overturning, shame will be gathered upon you, and upon your glory, which you at first believed you had; and this you will suffer because the impiety of Lebanon will cover you, according to what is said: And let his prayer become sin. For Lebanon, in the Greek language, is ὀμώνυμος (of the same name) with frankincense; and frankincense is a σύμβολον (a symbol) of the spiritual incense, which is the worship of God. Therefore the perverse prayer of the heretics, not directed by the simplicity of the Gospel, will be turned for them into sin, and the impiety of their worship of God will cover them. Hence there follows: And the misery of the beasts will terrify you because of the blood of men, and the impieties of the land, and of the city and of all who dwell in it. […]

2:17.t: For the iniquity of Lebanon will cover you: your pride, he says, and the overthrow of the temple, and the plundering of the sanctuary will lay you waste and devastate you. And because he had once named Mount Lebanon, under the metaphor of the same mountain he compares the victims and the sacrifices, or certainly the multitude of the peoples which was slain in Jerusalem, to animals or beasts, saying: And the devastation of the animals will crush you. But all this you will suffer because you laid waste Judah, overturned the land of promise, and the city of Jerusalem and all its inhabitants.

2:18.t: What does the graven image profit, since its maker has graven it, a molten thing and a false image? Since its maker has hoped in his own fashioning, so as to make dumb idols. LXX: What does the graven image profit, since they have graven it; they have formed it a molten thing, a false image? Since the maker trusts in his own fashioning, so as to make dumb idols. In sequence with what precedes, it is said of Nebuchadnezzar that he fashioned a statue of the idol Bel and set it up in the plain of Dura, or, as it is written in the Hebrew, Dora, about which we read more fully in Daniel. And so Scripture marvels at the madness and folly of the king, in that he himself ordered a golden statue to be made, and the maker trusts in the image that he has fashioned; and this we can indeed also take generally against all the worshipers of idols. Nor let us think that what is graven and what is molten are one and the same. […]

2:19.t: Woe to him who says to the wood: Wake up; arise, to the silent stone; can it teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and no spirit at all is in its inward parts. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before his face. LXX: Woe to him who says to the wood: Awake and rise up, and to the stone: Be lifted up. And it is an image, and it is a beaten work of gold and silver, and no spirit at all is in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth revere him before his face. This too can likewise be taken either against Nebuchadnezzar or against all who venerate idols. And human error is described, in that men think the silver, gold, gems and silk with which the idols are either wrapped or covered to be gods, because of the brilliance of the material, although the craftsman could indeed give them form, but could not give the soul by which limbs are quickened.

But if anyone should object, how can it be said that there is no spirit in idols, when unclean spirits attend all images, let him learn the custom of holy Scripture: that a perverse spirit is never called spirit absolutely, but always with some addition, as there: They were led astray by a spirit of fornication. And in the Gospel: But when an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, and other things like these. But wherever spirit is read alone and absolutely, without any addition, it always refers to the good side, that is, to the Holy Spirit, as in that saying of the Apostle: He who sows in the Spirit will reap from the Spirit eternal life, and elsewhere: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, and in another place: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. Nor do we say this as though the Holy Spirit too were not set down with an addition: for he is called both the Holy Spirit, and the princely spirit, and the right spirit, and the spirit of God, and other things like these; […]

2:20.t: And then, as to that which is subjoined, "When the time is come, Thou shalt be shown forth," what exposition doth this require, if a man diligently direct the eye of his mind to the festival which we are now celebrating? "For then shalt Thou be shown forth," He says, "as upon a kingly charger, by Thy pure and chaste mother, in the temple, and that in the grace and beauty of the flesh assumed by Thee." All these things the prophet, summing up for the sake of greater clearness, exclaims in brief: "The Lord is in His holy temple;" "Fear before Him all the earth."

And on the contrary the Lord is said to be in his holy temple; not in a temple made by hands, but either in the heavens, or in each of the saints, according to the Apostle, who says: Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and the spirit of God dwells in you? And elsewhere: Your bodies are the temple of God; or in the Son, as he himself says: The Father who abides in me, he does the works. Or certainly according to that saying, that the heavens and the lands, the seas and the whole world:

A spirit within sustains them, and mind, poured through all the limbs,

moves the whole mass, and mingles itself with the great body.

The whole world, which consists of heaven and earth and is enclosed by the circles of the heavens, is said to be the house of God. Hence the Apostle too says confidently: For in him, he says, we live, and move, and are.

3:1.t: The prophet Habakkuk gives this title to his canticle: "A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet for ignorance." For he had spoken in a bold manner to the Lord and had said, "How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? Shall I cry to you 'suffering violence,' and you will not save? Why have you shown me iniquity and grievance, to see rapine and injustice before me? Judgment is done against me and opposition is more powerful. Therefore the law is torn to pieces, and judgment comes not to the end, because the wicked prevails against the just; therefore, wrong judgment goes forth." As a reproof to himself for having spoken these words through ignorance, he writes the Canticle of Penance. If ignorance were no sin, it was a futile effort on his part to compose a book of penance, and his desire to express sorrow over an act that was not a sin was an empty gesture.

A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet for ignorances. LXX: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet with a song. Aquila and Symmachus and the Fifth Edition translated, as we did, for ignorances; Theodotion alone ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐκουσιασμῶν, that is, for voluntary sins, and for those who sin of their own accord. This is said so that we may understand — the Seventy excepted — that no one translated a prayer with a song. For in the Hebrew too it has al segionoth, which is rendered Ἐπὶ ἀγνοημάτων, and we translated for ignorances. Now the sense is this: earlier he had rashly said: How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? Shall I cry out to you, suffering violence, and you will not save? And then, in the second complaint: Why do you not look upon those who act unjustly, and keep silent, while the wicked devours one more just than himself? To this he had heard: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets. And after other things: Behold, he who is unbelieving, his soul will not be upright in himself; […]

3:2.t: With Him is nothing incomplete or out of due season, just as with the Father there is nothing incongruous. For all these things were foreknown by the Father; but the Son works them out at the proper time in perfect order and sequence. This was the reason why, when Mary was urging [Him] on to [perform] the wonderful miracle of the wine, and was desirous before the time to partake of the cup of emblematic significance, the Lord, checking her untimely haste, said, "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come" -waiting for that hour which was foreknown by the Father. This is also the reason why, when men were often desirous to take Him, it is said, "No man laid hands upon Him, for the hour of His being taken was not yet come;" nor the time of His passion, which had been foreknown by the Father; as also says the prophet Habakkuk, "By this Thou shalt be known when the years have drawn nigh; Thou shalt be set forth when the time comes; because my soul is disturbed by anger, Thou shalt remember Thy mercy." […]

The Father gave to the Son new disciples after Moses and Elijah had been exhibited along with him in the honor of his glory and had then been dismissed as having fully discharged their duty and office.… But we have the entire structure of this same vision in Habakkuk also, where the spirit in the person of some of the apostles says, "O Lord, I have heard your speech and was afraid." What speech was this, other than the words of the voice from heaven, "This is my beloved Son, hear him"? "I considered your works and was astonished." When could this have better happened than when Peter, on seeing his glory, knew not what he was saying? "In the midst of the two you shall be known"—even Moses and Elijah.

And we think that the expression also which occurs in the hymn of Habakkuk, "In the midst either of the two living things, or of the two lives, you will be known," ought to be understood of Christ and the Holy Spirit. For all knowledge of the Father is obtained by revelation of the Son through the Holy Spirit, so that both of these beings which, according to the prophet, are called either "living things" or "lives" exist as the grounds of the knowledge of God the Father. For it is said of the Son that "no one knows the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him." The same also is said by the apostle of the Holy Spirit, when he declares, "God has revealed them to us by his Holy Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." And again in the Gospel, when the Savior speaks of the divine and profounder parts of his teaching, which his disciples were not yet able to receive, he thus addresses them: "I cannot bear them now; […]

[Passage quoted, Hab. iii. 2-5.]

LISTENING to himself, or rather to the divine prophetic spirit within him, which said of the subject of the prophecy, "He that cometh will come, and will not tarry, and the just shall live by my faith," and believing as a just man in the oracle, the holy prophet says in the passage before us, "O Lord, I have heard thy report, and I was afraid," and the words that follow in which he clearly announces that God will come to men.

And who could this be who was known of old, and was to be known afterwards when the time drew near, and was to be shewn forth at the date predicted, but that same Being before shewn to be the second Lord of the Universe, who agreeably to the prophecy at the end of the ages has been proclaimed for all to hear? […]
3:2.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 15

3:2.t: O Lord, I have heard your hearing, and I was afraid. O Lord, your work, in the midst of the years, revive it. LXX: O Lord, I have heard your report, and I was afraid. O Lord, I considered your works, and I was astonished; in the midst of two living creatures you will be known. Where we and Aquila and Theodotion translated revive it, Symmachus rendered revive it again. But what the Seventy said, I considered and I was astonished, is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any of the other translators, so that, when the things not found in the Hebrew are removed, one can read according to the Seventy: O Lord, your works in the midst of two living creatures you will be known; and because this seemed ἀδιανόητον (unintelligible), the preceding words were joined to it. Now we read in the Hebrew adonai, that is, O Lord, phalach, your work, bacereb, in the midst, sanim, of years heieu, revive it. This is said so that we may recognize that what is superfluous in the Seventy has plainly been added. […]

This then we think should be above all else observed by those who want to keep the affec- tion of their companions unimpaired; viz., that first of all when provoked by any wrongs, a monk should keep not only his lips but even the depth of his breast unmoved: but if he finds that they are even slightly disturbed, let him keep himself in by entire silence, and diligently observe what the Psalmist speaks of: "I was troubled and spake nothing;" and: "I said I will take heed to thy ways that I offend not with my tongue. I have set a guard to my mouth, when the sinner stood against me. I was dumb and was humbled, and kept silence from good things;" and he should not pay any heed to his present state, nor give vent to what his violent rage suggests and his exasperated mind expresses at the moment, but should dwell on the grace of past love or look forward in his mind to the renewal and restoration of peace, and contemplate it even in the very hour of rage, as if it were sure presently to return. […]
3:2.s: The First Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 26

3:2.t: Lord, I heard Your report and feared. The report of the Lord the Savior is what He heard from the Father, that He would come in the flesh, be born into the world, dwell among the weak as the Almighty, among sinners as the Just, among men as God, perform heavenly works, teach heavenly precepts, promise heavenly gifts, be tempted, scourged, mocked, killed, and by His death destroy our death; rising from the dead, ascend into the heavens, and having sent the Spirit from above, illuminate the world with the grace of truth. Of this report He Himself frequently made mention in the Gospel, saying: "But He that sent me is true, and I speak to the world those things which I have heard of Him" (John 8:26). And again: "But I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you" (John 15:15). Concerning this, John the Baptist also says: "He that comes from heaven is above all, and what He has seen and heard, that He testifies" (John 3:31). […]
3:2.s: Commentary on the Song of Habakkuk

3:2.t: I considered Your works and was afraid: surely those works by which He redeemed the world, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross: that, as the Apostle again says, through death He might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). Indeed, the more one diligently considers these works, the more one trembles at the works of one's own frailty.
3:2.s: Commentary on the Song of Habakkuk

3:2.t: In the midst of two animals you will be known. It can be understood as in the midst of two animals, in the midst of Moses and Elijah. For there he was known to the three disciples on the holy mountain because he was to die, telling them that he would suffer in Jerusalem.
